newsitem.title: UK: Fishermen still shut UK oil port despite move order.
newsitem.headline: Fishermen still shut UK oil port despite move order.

text.p: A small group of fishermen said on Tuesday it was still blocking the strategic oil port of Sullom Voe in the Shetlands despite receiving a compsulory order to move their vessels out of the harbour on the second day of the blockade.
But they will move when legal documents backing the order are presented to them by the police, the group said.
The compulsory order or "special directive" was issued by the Sheltands Islands Council at 2130 local time (2030 GMT) on Monday ordering the fishing boats to leave the port area by 0300 on Tuesday.
"We are still here and won't move until the police bring legal documents," a crew member of one of the blockading boats told Reuters by mobile telephone.
A small group of shell fishermen took on the might of the international oil industry on Monday in a protest against unpaid compensation claims from the Braer tanker spill four years ago.
The boats blockaded the strategic Shetland oil port of Sullom Voe in the North Sea, which handles about one-fifth of Britain's oil output.
On Tuesday morning a tanker is scheduled to leave the port and another is expected to arrive in the afternoon, according to port authorities.
Sullom Voe is the export terminal for world benchmark North Sea Brent crude, exporting an average of about 480,000 barrels of crude per day.
The Shetland Islands Council owns and operates the Sullom Voe port under a special act of parliament that includes the power to issue a "special directive".

The crews of the boats are protesting against the failure of the International Oil Pollution Compensation Fund (IOPCF) to pay compensation in full for pollution caused to fishing grounds around the islands by oil spilt from the Braer in January 1993.

"(The IOPCF) has consistently denied that any long term damage has been done...But the (fishing) grounds up here are still affected and our livelihood is being destroyed," a fisherman aboard one of the blockading boats said on Monday.

The blockaders are demanding immediate payment of compensation claims for the past 18 months plus a scientific survey of shellfish stocks to ascertain the level of damage caused by the 85,000 tonne oil spill.
"The council has every sympathy with the fishermen who are protesting against the IOPC but this is not they way to do it," said Green.
He said a "special directive" meant the fishing boats would have to leave the harbour area or face criminal and civil charges.
If the boats didn't leave it "would become a matter for the police," said Green, adding that possible civil penalties might include the cost of delaying huge ocean going oil tankers.
